text: What are the key stages of design thinking in the correct order?
optionA: Define → Empathise → Ideate → Refine → Realise → Test
optionB: Empathise → Define → Ideate → Refine → Realise → Test
optionC: Ideate → Define → Empathise → Refine → Test → Realise
optionD: Research → Brief → Specification → Design → Make → Test
explanation: The 9705 design thinking stages: Empathise (research users' needs) → Define (state problems) → Ideate (create ideas) → Refine (develop iteratively) → Realise (create solutions) → Test (try solutions).

text: What is the difference between iterative design and intuitive design?
optionA: Iterative uses CAD; intuitive uses hand drawing
optionB: Iterative repeatedly tests and refines designs through cycles of feedback; intuitive relies on designer instinct and experience without systematic testing
optionC: Iterative is for products; intuitive is for graphics
optionD: Iterative is slower; intuitive produces better outcomes
explanation: Iterative design cycles through design-test-refine repeatedly; improving the product each time. Intuitive design relies on the designer's feel and experience rather than systematic testing.

text: What is a Gantt chart used for in product design?
optionA: Showing the manufacturing cost breakdown
optionB: Planning and tracking project tasks over time; showing what happens simultaneously and what must happen in sequence
optionC: Communicating the design to the client using 3D drawings
optionD: Analysing competitors' products against a specification
explanation: A Gantt chart is a bar chart showing project tasks against a timeline — it shows duration; overlap; and sequence; helping teams manage resources and meet deadlines.

text: What is a design specification?
optionA: A list of tools and materials needed to make a product
optionB: A set of measurable; justified criteria that a successful design must meet; derived from the design brief and research
optionC: A marketing description of the product's features
optionD: A technical drawing showing dimensions of the product
explanation: A design specification sets measurable success criteria (size; weight; cost; function; materials) so that any proposed solution can be objectively tested against it.

text: What is the purpose of a materials/cutting list in production planning?
optionA: To identify which tools are unsafe to use
optionB: A table specifying every material required: type; quantity; dimensions; and sometimes cost — enabling efficient preparation and ordering
optionC: A list of techniques used to shape materials
optionD: A specification of which machines are on the production floor
explanation: A cutting list (or materials list) prevents waste and shortages by detailing every component's material; quantity and dimensions before manufacture begins.

text: In the design process; what is the purpose of modelling?
optionA: To create the final marketable product
optionB: To physically or digitally test the viability; appearance; and function of a design idea before committing to full manufacture
optionC: To produce working drawings for the manufacturer
optionD: To complete the product analysis report
explanation: Modelling (prototypes; mock-ups; CAD renders) is exploratory — it identifies problems cheaply and quickly; reducing costly mistakes later in full production.

text: What is a flowchart used for in design and technology?
optionA: Showing the aesthetic arrangement of a product
optionB: Representing the sequence of steps in a manufacturing process or decision logic using standardised symbols
optionC: Presenting the colour scheme of a product
optionD: Mapping the target market demographics
explanation: Flowcharts use standard symbols (ovals for start/end; rectangles for processes; diamonds for decisions) to map manufacturing sequences or quality inspection logic.

text: What is the difference between quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC)?
optionA: QA is done by customers; QC is done by designers
optionB: QA checks are applied at every stage of the production process to prevent defects; QC checks are applied to the finished product to detect defects
optionC: QC is more thorough than QA in all situations
optionD: QA only applies to materials; QC only applies to assembly
explanation: QA is proactive — built into every production stage to prevent defects occurring. QC is reactive — checking finished products against standards and rejecting failures.

text: What is Total Quality Management (TQM)?
optionA: A government regulation for product safety standards
optionB: A management philosophy where quality assurance procedures are applied throughout the entire production process and organisation
optionC: A type of quality control test applied only to finished products
optionD: A certification issued by ISO to approved manufacturers
explanation: TQM involves everyone in an organisation taking responsibility for quality — from design to delivery — not just a separate quality department. It aims for continuous improvement.

text: What does ISO stand for and what is its role in product quality?
optionA: International Standards Organisation — sets global safety requirements
optionB: International Organization for Standardization — sets internationally agreed standards for quality; safety; and performance of products and processes
optionC: International School of Operations — trains quality inspectors
optionD: Independent Safety Office — audits manufacturing facilities
explanation: ISO develops and publishes international standards (e.g. ISO 9001 for quality management systems) that give buyers and regulators confidence that products meet consistent requirements.

text: During product analysis; which ten aspects should be evaluated?
optionA: Function; material; colour; brand; price; popularity; age; shape; smell; weight
optionB: Function; aesthetics; ergonomics; materials; production processes; target market; cost; safety; quality control; sustainability
optionC: Design; communication; planning; making; testing; reflecting; iterating; reviewing; revising; finishing
optionD: Style; innovation; culture; environment; fashion; trends; availability; regulation; ethics; impact
explanation: The 9705 syllabus specifies this list of ten product analysis dimensions — each gives a different perspective on how well the product serves its purpose and users.

text: What is a product extension strategy?
optionA: Increasing the size of a product
optionB: Actions taken when a product enters its decline stage to extend its commercial life; such as discounting; updating packaging; or adding features
optionC: A plan for adding new products to a company's range
optionD: A technique for testing product durability
explanation: In the product life cycle; decline = falling sales. Extension strategies (new variants; redesigned packaging; price reductions; new markets) aim to lift sales back up without full redesign.

text: What is an isometric drawing?
optionA: A 2D drawing showing only front and side views
optionB: A 3D drawing in which all three axes are drawn at equal 30° angles to the horizontal; with all edges drawn to true length
optionC: A drawing showing internal cross-sections of a product
optionD: A view looking down from directly above a product
explanation: Isometric projection shows three faces of an object simultaneously at 30° angles — it gives a 3D impression while keeping all measurements true; making it easy to draw accurately.

text: What is first angle orthographic projection?
optionA: A 3D drawing with perspective lines converging to two vanishing points
optionB: A system of drawing where the view is projected onto a plane placed on the FAR side of the object — the front view is top-left; side view top-right
optionC: A system where the view is projected onto a plane on the NEAR side of the object
optionD: A type of exploded view showing how parts connect
explanation: First angle (BS/ISO standard): Front view top-left → projects right to plan; right to left side view. Used in Europe/Asia. Third angle (US/UK engineering) is the alternative.

text: What does a sectional view in an orthographic drawing show?
optionA: The external surface finish of a product
optionB: An imaginary cut through the product to reveal internal features; with cross-hatching showing solid material
optionC: The assembly sequence for the product
optionD: The scale factor used in the drawing
explanation: Sectional views cut away part of the product to show internal shapes; holes; and features that would otherwise be hidden — essential for manufactured components.

text: What is a planometric (oblique) drawing and at what angles are the axes?
optionA: A 3D drawing with one axis at 45° and depth exaggerated
optionB: A 3D drawing with the plan view drawn true-shape horizontally and two vertical axes projected at 45° to the horizontal
optionC: A perspective drawing with one vanishing point
optionD: A freehand sketch used for quick ideation
explanation: Planometric (45/45) draws the top plan true-shape and projects left and right sides at 45° — popular for architectural and interior layouts because it preserves plan proportions.

text: What is an exploded view drawing?
optionA: A drawing showing a product after it has broken
optionB: A drawing where components are drawn separated along their assembly axes to show how they fit together
optionC: A view showing the internal cross-section of a component
optionD: A freehand sketch showing the product in context
explanation: Exploded views pull components apart along their assembly axes — used in manuals; instruction leaflets; and design portfolios to explain assembly and show individual parts.

text: What is the purpose of a development (net) drawing in graphic design?
optionA: To show the 3D form of a product using a perspective view
optionB: A flat 2D pattern that can be cut and folded to create a 3D form such as a box; prism; cone or cylinder
optionC: A scale drawing for a CNC cutting machine
optionD: A colour rendering of a product's surface finish
explanation: A net/development is a flat template showing every face joined together — with score lines for folds and glue/tab positions — so the form can be accurately manufactured.

text: What is vacuum forming used to produce?
optionA: Metal sheet components formed under high pressure
optionB: Hollow or concave thermoplastic parts by heating a plastic sheet and drawing it over a former using vacuum pressure
optionC: Solid 3D polymer parts by injecting molten plastic into a mould
optionD: Paper products by pressing wet pulp into a former
explanation: Vacuum forming: heat thermoplastic sheet → drape over a former (mould) → apply vacuum → plastic conforms to the mould → cool and trim. Used for packaging; trays; product housings.

text: What is the difference between injection moulding and blow moulding?
optionA: Injection moulding makes hollow containers; blow moulding makes solid parts
optionB: Injection moulding forces molten plastic into a closed mould to make solid parts; blow moulding inflates a hot plastic pre-form into a hollow container
optionC: Injection moulding uses thermosetting plastics; blow moulding uses thermoplastics
optionD: Both are identical processes used for the same applications
explanation: Injection moulding → solid parts (housings; brackets). Blow moulding → hollow containers (bottles; tanks). Both are high-volume; automated polymer processing methods.

text: What is annealing used for in metalworking?
optionA: Hardening metal to increase wear resistance
optionB: Heating metal and then slowly cooling it to relieve internal stresses and restore ductility and workability after cold working
optionC: Applying a rust-resistant coating to steel
optionD: Joining two metals by heating a filler rod
explanation: Cold working (bending; hammering) makes metal brittle. Annealing (heat to critical temperature → slow cool in sand or oven) restores ductility so the metal can be worked further without cracking.

text: What is line bending used for?
optionA: Joining two sheets of plastic with solvent adhesive
optionB: Heating a thermoplastic sheet along a straight line using a strip heater and then bending it to a precise angle
optionC: Cutting plastic sheet using a scored line and snapping
optionD: Forming a smooth curve in sheet metal using a roller
explanation: Line bending uses a strip heater (resistance element) to soften an acrylic or thermoplastic sheet along a precise line — allowing accurate angle bends for display stands; boxes; and guards.

text: What is the CYMK colour model used for in printing?
optionA: Describing screen colours in digital design
optionB: Colour separation for printing: Cyan; Yellow; Magenta and Key (black) inks are layered to reproduce full-colour images
optionC: Specifying paint colours for product finishing
optionD: Calibrating a 3D printer's colour output
explanation: CMYK subtractive colour: Cyan/Magenta/Yellow/Key (black) are the four ink channels in four-colour offset; digital; and screen printing. Separating into CMYK plates reproduces full colour.

text: What is the difference between soldering and welding?
optionA: Soldering joins metals permanently; welding is temporary
optionB: Soldering uses a low-melting-point filler metal to join components without melting the parent material; welding melts and fuses the parent materials together
optionC: Welding is used for plastics; soldering for metals
optionD: Soldering requires higher temperatures than welding
explanation: Soldering (< 450°C): filler only melts — parent metals stay solid; used for electronics and plumbing. Welding (> 450°C/brazing; MIG/TIG): melts parent metals for a stronger structural joint.

text: What is a thermoplastic?
optionA: A plastic that cannot be melted once set
optionB: A plastic that softens when heated and re-hardens when cooled; allowing it to be repeatedly reshaped
optionC: A plastic reinforced with glass fibre
optionD: A fully biodegradable plant-based polymer
explanation: Thermoplastics (acrylic; nylon; PVC; polypropylene; polyethylene) can be repeatedly melted and resolidified — making them recyclable. Thermosetting plastics cross-link permanently and cannot be remelted.

text: What is a composite material?
optionA: A material made from a single polymer
optionB: A material made by combining two or more materials with different properties to achieve improved overall performance
optionC: A metal alloy created by mixing two or more metals
optionD: A biodegradable material made from natural sources
explanation: Composites (GRP; CFRP; MDF; plywood) combine a matrix and a reinforcement — combining the best properties of both. E.g. CFRP: strong/stiff carbon fibres + lightweight/tough epoxy resin.

text: What is a smart material?
optionA: A material made using nanotechnology
optionB: A material that responds reversibly to a change in environmental conditions; such as temperature; light or stress
optionC: A material that is entirely recyclable
optionD: A material with significantly lower density than traditional alternatives
explanation: Smart materials respond reversibly: shape memory alloys (NiTi) return to original shape when heated; thermochromic pigments change colour with temperature; photochromic lenses darken in UV light.

text: What is the difference between a hardwood and a softwood?
optionA: Hardwoods are always harder than softwoods
optionB: Hardwoods come from deciduous (broad-leaved) trees; softwoods from coniferous (cone-bearing) trees — the terms describe tree type; not necessarily hardness
optionC: Softwoods are more sustainable; hardwoods less so
optionD: Softwoods are used for furniture; hardwoods for construction
explanation: Balsa is a 'hardwood' but is lighter than many 'softwoods'. The classification is biological: deciduous (oak; beech; ash) = hardwood; coniferous (pine; cedar; fir) = softwood.

text: Which of the following is a biodegradable material?
optionA: Acrylic (PMMA)
optionB: Polylactide (PLA)
optionC: High-density polyethylene (HDPE)
optionD: Polycarbonate (PC)
explanation: PLA (polylactide) is a biodegradable thermoplastic derived from corn/potato starch that breaks down through microbial action. Standard petroleum-based polymers like HDPE and acrylic do not biodegrade.

text: What is the purpose of reducing the number of manufacturing processes when designing for sustainability?
optionA: To make the product cheaper to buy
optionB: To reduce energy consumption; waste; pollution; and production time; lowering the product's overall environmental impact
optionC: To allow more complex products to be designed
optionD: To increase the life span of the product
explanation: Every manufacturing process uses energy; creates waste; and can generate pollution. Designing to minimise processes (fewer cuts; fewer coatings; fewer assemblies) reduces the carbon footprint.

text: What does 'ductility' mean as a material property?
optionA: The ability of a material to resist scratching
optionB: The ability of a material to be drawn into wire or stretched under tensile stress without fracturing
optionC: The ability of a material to return to its original shape after deformation
optionD: The ability of a material to absorb impact energy without fracturing
explanation: Ductile materials (copper; aluminium; mild steel) can be drawn into wire or pressed into shapes. Opposite is brittle (glass; cast iron) which fractures without plastic deformation.

text: What is Just-In-Time (JIT) manufacturing?
optionA: A system of quality control that checks parts as they are made
optionB: A production philosophy where materials and components are delivered exactly when needed; eliminating storage costs but requiring reliable supply chains
optionC: A method of rapid 3D printing for one-off production
optionD: A scheduling system using Gantt charts for batch production
explanation: JIT (Toyota origin) reduces inventory and storage costs by synchronising deliveries with production schedules. Risk: supply chain disruption immediately halts production.

text: What is Computer-Integrated Manufacturing (CIM)?
optionA: Using a computer to design products only
optionB: A system where computers control and coordinate all aspects of manufacturing — design; planning; production; quality control and logistics — in one integrated system
optionC: A type of 3D printing used only in aerospace
optionD: A system where human workers are managed by computer scheduling
explanation: CIM integrates CAD → CAM → automated inspection → logistics under one computer system — minimising human intervention; reducing errors; and enabling 24/7 production.

text: What is the difference between one-off; batch and mass production?
optionA: One-off is cheapest; mass production most expensive per unit
optionB: One-off (single custom item) is highest cost per unit; batch (set quantity at once then switch) is intermediate; mass (continuous high volume identical items) has lowest cost per unit
optionC: Batch production never uses automation; mass production always does
optionD: One-off production always uses CNC; batch uses hand tools
explanation: Scale of production is inversely linked to unit cost: one-off (bespoke; high labour) → batch (shared setup; medium volume) → mass (automated; lowest unit cost but no customisation).

text: What is Kaizen™ in manufacturing?
optionA: A Japanese word for quality control checking
optionB: A continuous improvement philosophy where all employees; at every level; seek to make small; incremental improvements to processes every day
optionC: A type of industrial robot used in Japanese factories
optionD: A just-in-time delivery scheduling system
explanation: Kaizen (改善 = "change for better") underpins Lean Manufacturing: every worker actively identifies and reports small process improvements — collectively producing major efficiency gains.

text: What is the marketing mix (4Ps)?
optionA: Price; People; Place; Promotion
optionB: Product; Price; Promotion; Place
optionC: Process; Price; Promotion; Packaging
optionD: Product; People; Profit; Place
explanation: The 4Ps: Product (what you sell); Price (how much); Promotion (how you tell people); Place (how/where it reaches customers). Marketing strategy requires balancing all four.

text: What is the product life cycle (in correct order)?
optionA: Introduction → Research → Growth → Maturity → Decline
optionB: Research & Development → Introduction → Growth → Maturity → Decline
optionC: Growth → Introduction → Maturity → R&D → Decline
optionD: Introduction → Growth → R&D → Maturity → Decline
explanation: Product life cycle: R&D (pre-launch investment) → Introduction (slow sales; high marketing cost) → Growth (rapid sales rise) → Maturity (peak; market saturation) → Decline (falling sales).

text: What is offset lithography used for?
optionA: Printing directly from a digital file onto paper
optionB: A large-scale commercial printing process where the inked image is transferred from a plate to a rubber blanket and then to the printing surface
optionC: Embossing a pattern into thick card for luxury packaging
optionD: Applying a metallic foil finish to printed card
explanation: Offset litho (the most common commercial printing method): aluminium plates → rubber blanket (offset) → paper. Economical at high volumes; excellent quality; used for books; magazines; packaging.

text: What does PPE stand for and when should it be worn?
optionA: Product Protection Equipment — when using hand tools
optionB: Personal Protective Equipment — worn whenever a process or material poses a risk to the body (eyes; skin; lungs; ears)
optionC: Proper Protective Enclosure — worn only during welding
optionD: Permitted Practice Equipment — only required by regulations in a commercial factory
explanation: PPE (goggles; gloves; face mask; apron; ear defenders) is selected based on the specific hazard — a risk assessment identifies which PPE is needed for each task.

text: What is a risk assessment?
optionA: A list of all the tools in a workshop
optionB: A systematic process of identifying hazards; evaluating the likelihood and severity of harm; and implementing control measures to reduce risk
optionC: A health and safety certificate required for all teachers
optionD: A record of past accidents in the workshop
explanation: Risk assessments: identify hazard → who might be harmed → evaluate risk (likelihood × severity) → control measures (guards; PPE; training; supervision) → review. Required by law in most countries.

text: Which of the following is a correct health and safety practice when using a pillar drill?
optionA: Remove the safety guard for a clearer view
optionB: Secure the workpiece with a clamp or machine vice; never hold it by hand
optionC: Hold long hair loosely to one side; do not tie it back
optionD: Increase speed for harder materials to get through faster
explanation: A rotating drill bit can grab a loose workpiece and spin it violently. Clamping prevents this. Long hair must be tied back (not just to the side) to prevent entanglement with rotating machinery.

text: Why should welding goggles be worn for arc welding but not for general workshop use?
optionA: Welding goggles improve peripheral vision
optionB: Arc welding produces ultraviolet and infrared radiation that can permanently damage unprotected eyes — standard safety glasses do not filter these wavelengths
optionC: Welding goggles are more comfortable than safety glasses
optionD: Workshop regulations require different PPE for each country
explanation: Arc welding emits intense UV and IR radiation (arc flash) — even brief unprotected exposure can cause "arc eye" (photokeratitis). Welding goggles have specific shade ratings for each welding process.

text: What is a composite material combining glass fibres in a polyester resin matrix called?
optionA: Medium density fibreboard (MDF)
optionB: Glass fibre reinforced plastic (GRP)
optionC: Carbon fibre reinforced plastic (CFRP)
optionD: Engineered wood
explanation: GRP (fibreglass) = E-glass fibres + polyester or epoxy resin matrix. Lightweight; strong; corrosion-resistant — used for boats; car body panels; swimming pools; helmets.

text: What property does 'toughness' describe in materials science?
optionA: The ability to resist permanent deformation under load
optionB: The ability to absorb energy and resist fracture when subjected to sudden impact or shock loading
optionC: The ability to be stretched into wire without breaking
optionD: The hardness of a material measured by scratch resistance
explanation: Toughness is energy absorbed before fracture (area under stress-strain curve). Tough materials (mild steel; ABS) resist sudden shocks. Hard materials can be brittle (glass; hardened steel).

text: What is carbon fibre reinforced plastic (CFRP) used for and what are its main advantages?
optionA: Structural concrete reinforcement — cheap and abundant
optionB: High-performance products (aircraft; sports cars; bicycles; prosthetics) — extremely high strength-to-weight ratio and stiffness
optionC: Food packaging — fully biodegradable
optionD: Electrical wiring insulation — excellent electrical resistance
explanation: CFRP combines the extreme stiffness and strength of carbon fibre with the low density and toughness of polymer matrix — producing the highest strength-to-weight ratio of any structural material.

text: What does 'malleability' mean as a material property?
optionA: The ability to be pulled into wire
optionB: The ability to be pressed; beaten or rolled into thin sheets without fracturing
optionC: Resistance to corrosion in acidic environments
optionD: The springiness of a material when compressed
explanation: Malleable materials (gold; aluminium; mild steel) deform under compressive forces — enabling hammering; rolling; and pressing into sheets. Copper is both ductile and malleable.

text: What are the three main sources of renewable energy?
optionA: Coal; oil and natural gas
optionB: Uranium; thorium and plutonium
optionC: Water; wind and solar
optionD: Coal; wood and biomass
explanation: The 9705 syllabus specifies water (hydroelectric); wind (wind turbines); and solar (photovoltaic/thermal) as renewable energy sources — in contrast to finite fossil fuels (oil; natural gas; coal).

text: What is the purpose of a feedback loop in a control system?
optionA: To amplify the input signal to a higher voltage
optionB: To use the output of a system to automatically adjust the input; keeping the output within a desired range
optionC: To convert electrical energy into mechanical motion
optionD: To measure how much energy a system consumes
explanation: Feedback (closed-loop control): sensor detects output → compares to set point → error signal → controller adjusts actuator input. Example: thermostat; cruise control; CNC machine.

text: What is CAD (Computer-Aided Design) used for in product design?
optionA: Manufacturing products directly using computer-controlled machines
optionB: Using software to create; store; modify and analyse product designs digitally — producing technical drawings; 3D models and simulations
optionC: Testing products for safety using physical prototypes
optionD: Managing a factory's production schedule
explanation: CAD (SolidWorks; AutoCAD; Fusion 360; Adobe Illustrator) enables faster iteration; accurate dimensioned drawings; 3D visualisation; material simulation; and digital sharing with manufacturers.

text: What is the difference between CAD and CAM?
optionA: CAD is expensive; CAM is cheaper
optionB: CAD designs the product digitally; CAM uses digital design data to directly control machines (CNC routers; laser cutters; 3D printers) in manufacturing
optionC: CAM stands for Computer-Aided Marketing
optionD: CAD is used only for graphics; CAM for engineering only
explanation: The CAD-CAM workflow: design in CAD → export toolpath data (G-code) → send to CAM machine (CNC lathe; laser cutter; 3D printer) which manufactures the part automatically.

text: What is rapid prototyping and why is it valuable?
optionA: The process of quickly training workers on the production line
optionB: Using processes such as 3D printing to produce a physical model of a design quickly and cheaply to test form; fit and function before committing to tooling
optionC: A shortcut to producing the final product without testing
optionD: A method of rapid chemical surface treatment for metals
explanation: Rapid prototyping (3D printing; SLA; SLS) produces test parts in hours without expensive tooling — allowing designers to identify and fix problems early when changes are cheapest.

text: What is an LDR (Light Dependent Resistor) and how does it work?
optionA: A component that changes colour in response to light
optionB: A resistor whose resistance decreases as light intensity increases — used as a light sensor in automatic street lights and camera exposure meters
optionC: A resistor that only works in direct current circuits
optionD: A component that emits light when current flows through it
explanation: LDR (photoresistor): high light → low resistance; low light → high resistance. Used in light-sensing circuits where the LDR is part of a potential divider to trigger switching circuits.

text: What is the function of a transistor in an electronic control circuit?
optionA: To store electrical charge
optionB: To act as a switch or amplifier — a small base current controls a much larger collector-emitter current; enabling logic outputs to drive motors or lamps
optionC: To convert AC to DC
optionD: To filter out unwanted high frequencies from a signal
explanation: A transistor as a switch: when base voltage > ~0.7V; transistor saturates (fully ON) and allows collector-emitter current to flow — allowing a low-power microcontroller to switch high-power loads.

text: What does a capacitor do in an electronic circuit?
optionA: Converts voltage to current
optionB: Stores electrical charge (energy); releasing it later — used for smoothing power supplies; timing circuits; and filtering
optionC: Increases resistance to limit current
optionD: Converts electrical energy to magnetic energy
explanation: A capacitor (farads F) stores charge on two conducting plates separated by a dielectric. Charge/discharge time constant RC = resistance × capacitance — used in timers; filters; oscillators.

text: What is an actuator in a control system?
optionA: A device that senses conditions such as temperature or light
optionB: A device that converts an electrical signal into a physical action — such as a motor; solenoid; heater; buzzer or lamp
optionC: The microcontroller that processes input signals
optionD: The power supply that drives the control circuit
explanation: In INPUT → PROCESS → OUTPUT: actuators are the output devices that cause the system to do something in the physical world. Examples: DC motor; servo motor; relay; LED; solenoid valve.

text: What is RFID (Radio Frequency Identification) used for in manufacturing and retail?
optionA: Wireless internet access for factory computers
optionB: Tracking products; components and assets using radio waves — a tag on the item broadcasts its ID to a reader without line-of-sight or physical contact
optionC: Encrypting communications between factory machines
optionD: Remote control of CNC machines using radio signals
explanation: RFID tags (passive or active) enable automated inventory tracking; supply chain management; anti-theft systems; and product provenance verification without manual scanning.

text: What is augmented reality (AR) used for in product design?
optionA: Replacing physical prototypes entirely in all cases
optionB: Overlaying digital information (3D models; instructions; data) onto the real world view through a camera or headset — enabling designers to visualise products in real environments before manufacture
optionC: Controlling CNC machines through hand gestures
optionD: Communicating with suppliers using encrypted video calls
explanation: AR allows designers and clients to see how a product will look and fit in its real environment before manufacture — reducing costly design errors and improving client communication.
